name: GABA supplement

lead: GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter, and capsules or powders of it are sold as supplements for relaxation and sleep. Looksmaxxing posts are brief, mostly users saying they ordered it to feel calmer and more at ease around people, which shows up as better social presence.

Whether oral GABA reaches the brain is debated: the traditional view is that it crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, while rat studies from the 2010s have made that unclear. Small registered trials cover insomnia, glucose control and menopausal symptoms; none targets appearance.

paras: It is taken as capsules or powder, usually in the evening for sleep or before social situations for calm. Users judge it by how relaxed they feel.

Reference sources advise against use in pregnancy and lactation because of possible effects on growth hormone and other safety concerns. Supplement quality is not regulated like medicines, and no standard clinical guidance exists.

social.title: Unhealthy diet associated with altered gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamate

angle.text: Users take GABA supplements for calm, sleep and social ease, hoping to come across as more relaxed and confident. Whether oral GABA reaches the brain is debated, and small trials cover sleep and glucose, not appearance.

lead: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian central nervous system and is also sold as an oral dietary supplement in many countries, usually in capsule or powder form marketed for relaxation and sleep.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities it appears mainly in short posts by users who say they ordered it to feel calmer and appear more relaxed around people they want to impress, a claimed route to better social presence and expression rather than a change to physical features.[2][3][4]

Whether orally taken GABA reaches the brain has long been questioned; Wikipedia notes the traditional view that it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, while rat studies from the 2010s have made this unclear.[1] Registered human studies of GABA supplements cover sleep, glucose control, cognition and menopausal symptoms.[5][6][7][8][9] No published trial addresses appearance.
infobox: Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mature mammalian CNS[1]
Sold as a dietary supplement in many countries[1]
Wikipedia advises against use in pregnancy and lactation[1]

paras: GABA is made in the brain from glutamic acid and acts to reduce neuronal excitability.[1] The same molecule is sold as a supplement. Products are sold for relaxation, which is the context in which looksmaxxing posters mention it.[2][3]

GABA is a white, water-soluble crystalline powder that exists mostly as a zwitterion. It is not an alpha-amino acid and is not incorporated into proteins.[1] It is found in plants and microbes; the article notes it is the most abundant amino acid in the apoplast of tomatoes and that enzyme technology has been used to raise GABA content in some seeds such as lupine, quinoa and cañahua.[1]

GABA was first synthesised in 1883 and was initially known only as a product of plant and microbial metabolism. In 1950 Eugene Roberts and Sam Frankel at Washington University School of Medicine used newly developed chromatography to show that it is made from glutamic acid and accumulates in the mammalian central nervous system. Canadian researchers had named an unidentified brain extract component 'Factor I' in 1954 and identified it as GABA by 1957, when it was shown to inhibit crayfish neurons; in 1959 researchers showed it acts at an inhibitory synapse on crayfish muscle fibres.[1]

In the mature mammalian nervous system GABA acts at GABA-A receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels, and at GABA-B receptors, which are G protein-coupled. The main result is reduced neuronal excitability, although in developing brains GABA is largely excitatory and shapes proliferation, migration and synapse formation. Outside the nervous system GABA is produced in pancreatic beta cells, where it helps suppress glucagon secretion, and it has immune-modulating effects.[1]

Many drugs act on this system: benzodiazepines, barbiturates, zolpidem-type drugs, alcohol and propofol enhance GABA-A activity, baclofen and phenibut act at GABA-B, and gabapentin and pregabalin are GABA analogues. Kava contains GABAergic compounds such as kavain.[1] Rodent studies have examined dietary GABA, for example against high-fat-diet oxidative stress and fluoride-induced liver damage.[10][11]

Wikipedia states that exogenous GABA was traditionally thought not to cross the blood-brain barrier, that data from 2010s rat research make the notion unclear, and that brain areas lacking an effective barrier, such as the periventricular nucleus, can be reached by systemically injected GABA.[1] It also reports that at least one study found oral GABA increased human growth hormone, and, citing the possibility of biphasic effects on growth hormone and other safety concerns, that use is not recommended during pregnancy and lactation.[1]

No clinical studies of GABA supplements for appearance outcomes or for social anxiety were found. Registered trials include a study in children with insomnia (n=206, started 2024, status unknown),[5] a 30-person study of a dietary supplement on sleep quality,[6] a study of oral GABA bioavailability from tomatoes in 12 people,[12] a 52-person trial in prediabetes,[13] trials in type 1 diabetes (n=30 and n=100),[14][7] a 70-person trial of a supplement containing PQQ, GABA, caffeine and B vitamins on cognition in postmenopausal women,[8] and a 112-person study of a GABA-containing product on menopausal symptoms.[9] Results are not given in the registry entries cited here.

On looksmax.org, a handful of short posts announce orders or deliveries of GABA, titled as 'no-value posts', with users saying they plan to take it before social encounters to appear more relaxed.[2][3][4] The posts contain no outcome reports.[2]
GABA is sold as a dietary supplement in many countries.[1] Prescription drugs that act on the GABA system, such as benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids, are separately regulated.
Compounds that act on the same system include phenibut, which acts at GABA-B, and picamilon, described as a GABA analogue or prodrug; alcohol is a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A.[1]

lore.intro: GABA is mentioned in short forum posts by users hoping to feel calm in social situations; the threads announce orders and deliveries and contain no reports of results.[2][3][4]
